question.prompt: Last year Isabella took \(7\) math tests and received \(7\) different scores, each an integer between \(91\) and \(100,\) inclusive. After each test she noticed that the average of her test scores was an integer. Her score on the seventh test was \(95.\) What was her score on the sixth test?

solutions.title: Bound the total score
solutions.explanation:
An integer average after \(k\) tests means that the sum of the first \(k\) scores is divisible by \(k\). Applying this to the last few tests sharply restricts the scores.

Let \(S\) be the sum of all seven scores. Since the scores are distinct, the smallest possible sum uses \(91\) through \(97\), and the largest uses \(94\) through \(100\). Thus
\[
658=\frac{7(91+97)}2\le S\le\frac{7(94+100)}2=679.
\]
The final average is an integer, so \(S\) is a multiple of \(7\). The complete list of possibilities in this range is
\[
S\in\{658,665,672,679\}.
\]
The seventh score was \(95\), so \(S-95\), the sum of the first six scores, must be divisible by \(6\). Subtracting \(95\) from the four candidates gives
\[
563,\quad570,\quad577,\quad584.
\]
Only \(570=6\cdot95\) is divisible by \(6\). Therefore the first six scores sum to \(570\).

The first five scores sum to a multiple of \(5\). Since \(570\) is also a multiple of \(5\), their difference, the sixth score, must be a multiple of \(5\). The only such scores from \(91\) through \(100\) are \(95\) and \(100\). The seventh score already used \(95\), and all scores are different, so the sixth score was \(\boxed{100}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
